content: Heavy menstrual bleeding (HMB) is a common condition among otherwise healthy women of reproductive age, significantly impacting their physical health and quality of life. Surgical interventions are typically considered a second-line treatment for HMB. Endometrial resection or ablation (EA/ER) involves removing or ablating the endometrial lining and is a less invasive option compared to hysterectomy. Hysterectomy, which involves the complete removal of the uterus, is considered the definitive treatment for HMB and can be performed via open abdominal surgery, minimally invasive techniques (laparoscopic or vaginal), or an unspecified route. Each surgical approach has distinct advantages and risks. The objective of this study was to compare the effectiveness, acceptability, and safety of EA/ER with different types of hysterectomy (open, minimally invasive, or unspecified) for the treatment of HMB. The analysis included 10 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving 1,966 participants. The evidence was graded as moderate, low, or very low certainty. Endometrial Resection/Ablation vs. Open Hysterectomy: Women undergoing EA/ER are less likely to perceive an improvement in HMB compared to those undergoing open hysterectomy (moderate-certainty evidence). EA/ER is associated with a 13% risk of requiring further surgery for treatment failure, compared to no risk in the open hysterectomy group (moderate-certainty evidence). Both treatments likely result in similar quality of life at two years and similar satisfaction rates at one year (moderate-certainty evidence). Serious adverse events may occur at similar rates between the two groups (low-certainty evidence). EA/ER likely allows for a quicker return to normal activities compared to open hysterectomy, with an average difference of 21 days (moderate-certainty evidence). Endometrial Resection/Ablation vs. Minimally Invasive Hysterectomy: The proportion of women perceiving improvement in HMB at two years may be similar between EA/ER and minimally invasive hysterectomy (low-certainty evidence). Blood loss may be higher in the EA/ER group, as measured by the Pictorial Blood Assessment Chart (low-certainty evidence). Quality of life at two years is likely lower in the EA/ER group compared to the minimally invasive hysterectomy group, based on validated scales (moderate-certainty evidence). EA/ER is associated with a higher risk of requiring further surgery for treatment failure compared to minimally invasive hysterectomy (moderate-certainty evidence). Serious adverse events likely occur at similar rates between the two groups (moderate-certainty evidence). Women undergoing EA/ER are less likely to be satisfied with their treatment at one year compared to those undergoing minimally invasive hysterectomy (moderate-certainty evidence). Data on the time to return to normal activities could not be pooled due to high variability, but individual studies consistently favored EA/ER for quicker recovery. Endometrial Resection/Ablation vs. Unspecified Route of Hysterectomy: EA/ER may result in a lower perception of improvement in HMB compared to hysterectomy performed via an unspecified route (low-certainty evidence). Quality of life at two years may be similar between the two groups, but general health improvement at one year may be lower in the EA/ER group (low-certainty evidence). EA/ER carries a 5.4% risk of requiring further surgery for treatment failure, compared to no risk in the hysterectomy group (moderate-certainty evidence). EA/ER is associated with a lower risk of serious adverse events compared to hysterectomy via an unspecified route (moderate-certainty evidence). Satisfaction rates at one year are likely similar between the two groups (moderate-certainty evidence). EA/ER may allow for a shorter time to return to normal activities, with an average difference of 18.9 days (low-certainty evidence). Conclusions: Endometrial resection/ablation (EA/ER) is a viable alternative to hysterectomy for the surgical treatment of HMB, but its effectiveness varies depending on the type of hysterectomy it is compared to. Women undergoing EA/ER are less likely to perceive improvement in HMB compared to those undergoing open or unspecified hysterectomy, but the outcomes may be similar when compared to minimally invasive hysterectomy. Quality of life with EA/ER is likely comparable to open and unspecified hysterectomy but lower than with minimally invasive hysterectomy. The risk of requiring further surgery for treatment failure is higher with EA/ER across all comparisons. Satisfaction rates are similar to open and unspecified hysterectomy but lower compared to minimally invasive hysterectomy. Serious adverse events occur at similar rates across all groups, though specific adverse events differ. EA/ER likely allows for a quicker return to normal activities compared to hysterectomy.
